Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 3-day history of watery to loose stools 4–5 ×/day, one vomit, possible low-grade fever, able to maintain oral fluids, no blood or mucus.  
• No recent travel or suspicious food.  
• Past asthma; uses an inhaler called “Lexapro.”  
• Father with hypertension; deceased from bowel cancer at 62.

Working diagnosis  
• Acute viral gastroenteritis – most consistent with short duration, systemic upset, and spontaneous improvement expected.

Differential considerations (from DDx)  
• Acute bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis – possible but lower likelihood given absence of high-risk food/travel and lack of blood/fever.  
• Medication-induced diarrhoea (if “Lexapro” = escitalopram) – low–medium likelihood; temporal pattern unclear.

Management  
• Education on hydration and oral rehydration salts (Dioralyte).  
• Advise soft/bland diet; avoid dairy, meat, fish, eggs until 48 h diarrhoea-free; use yogurt/probiotics to restore gut flora.  
• Safety-net: seek review if > 1 week diarrhoea, blood in stool, frequency ≥ 6–8/day, or signs of dehydration; stool sample and possible antibiotics if indicated.  
• No medications prescribed at this visit.  
• Review asthma medication name and ensure appropriate inhaler at next contact.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – High likelihood; classic short-term watery diarrhoea with mild systemic symptoms and no red flags.  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis – Medium likelihood; similar presentation but no clear exposure history.  
3. Medication-induced diarrhoea (escitalopram) – Low-Medium likelihood; patient reports using “Lexapro,” a drug associated with GI upset.
